Importantly, this phase is not intended to train the router’s complementary behavior, but rather to produce a stable routing mechanism aligned with expert specialization. During SFT, we jointly optimize the base LLM parameters θ LM \theta_{\text{LM}} and the routing projection W W using a combination of a standard language modeling loss and a routing loss. The language modeling loss ℒ LM ​ ( θ LM ; x , y ) \mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}(\theta_{\text{LM}};x,y) given the data point ( x , y ) (x,y) follows the standard SFT objective and encourages accurate next-token prediction on the training data. To enable the token-level routing ability, we introduce a routing loss that favors experts whose predictions are more consistent with the ground-truth sequence. However, not all tokens are informative for routing. Many tokens, such as punctuation or common function words, are predicted identically by all experts and therefore provide little signal about expert specialization. Supervising routing on these tokens can dominate the gradient and bias the router toward uninformative agreement patterns. To mitigate this issue, we restrict routing supervision to token positions where experts disagree.
